damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Room of Requirement arrival / DA reunion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Seamus actively explains the Room of Requirement's defences to Harry, Ron and Hermione with enthusiasm and authority: 'It's a proper hideout, as long as one of us stays in here, they can't get at us... You've just got to make sure you close the loopholes. Neville's the man!' He also asks eager, engaged questions ('What were you after?', 'What's the plan?') and delivers the wry realist line 'That's nothing to go on.' He is a participant with voice and standing in the group.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Seamus's first line on arrival is a throwaway joke at Aberforth's expense ('Not more of Aberforth's cooking, I hope. Be a surprise if we could digest it.') and his second contribution is the single line 'That's nothing to go on.' The entire explanation of the Room's defensive properties — his clearest moment of competent, knowledgeable speech in the book — is cut. His role is reduced to comic relief and a single sceptical quip.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to establish Seamus as a resilient, informed survivor who understands the Room and actively contributes information. The film strips that competence away, leaving only comedy. His character voice is flattened at the first meaningful opportunity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Room of Requirement: Seamus describes two weeks in hiding
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Seamus an extended speech describing life in the Room over nearly two weeks: makeshift hammocks, the bathroom that appeared when girls arrived, the general texture of DA resistance life. This grounds him as a long-term participant in the resistance, not a latecomer, and gives him narrative real estate.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This speech is entirely absent from the film corpus. The film provides no equivalent account of the DA's experience hiding in the Room. Seamus is present as a background figure but delivers no such testimony.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Removing this speech costs Seamus his primary moment of narrative weight in the book's Hogwarts section. It also erases the audience's understanding of what the DA endured before Harry's return, and Seamus's specific place in that story.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Dean's return / Seamus's reunion hug
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Seamus a brief but emotionally significant beat: 'Seamus gave a great roar of delight and ran to hug his best friend' when Dean arrives. This is the only direct expression of the Seamus–Dean friendship in the entire book corpus, and it is vivid and characterful.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Dean Thomas is listed as already present in the Room of Requirement when Harry arrives (Film Scene 4 notes 'Dean Thomas' among the faces). There is no equivalent reunion moment between Seamus and Dean, and no expression of their friendship.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Seamus–Dean friendship is one of the few defined interpersonal bonds Seamus has in the books. Its sole expressive moment in this portion of the narrative is lost entirely, leaving their relationship invisible on screen.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Seamus casting a Patronus to repel Dementors
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book explicitly places Seamus among three DA members — Luna, Ernie, and Seamus — who arrive in the nick of time to cast Patronuses alongside Harry, Ron, and Hermione when their own Patronuses are failing. Seamus casts a silver fox Patronus. Ron then directly thanks Luna, Ernie, and Seamus. This is a clear moment of courage, magical competence, and active rescue.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire sequence — the Dementor attack, the failing Patronuses, and Seamus's timely arrival to help — does not appear in the film corpus. There is no corresponding scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is Seamus's single most significant act of agency in the book's battle sequence. He actively saves Harry, Ron, and Hermione. Its complete absence removes his only heroic set-piece in the Battle of Hogwarts, reducing him to a background combatant with no individual moment of courage or magical achievement during the battle proper.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Neville's speech to Voldemort / 'Stand down, Neville!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book there is no equivalent scene where Seamus angrily tells Neville to stand down. In the book's equivalent moment, Neville acts autonomously and the crowd's reaction is not characterised by Seamus opposing him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film (Scene 13), when Neville begins his speech to Voldemort, Seamus shouts 'Stand down, Neville!' angrily and tries to physically push forward, only stopped by Ron gripping his arm. This presents Seamus as someone who would capitulate or prevent defiance at the story's most critical moment of collective courage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents a moment of cowardice or defeatism for Seamus at the saga's climactic turning point. In the books he is a Gryffindor fighter who casts Patronuses to save Harry; here he is the voice urging surrender. This actively contradicts his established characterisation and damages his integrity at the worst possible narrative moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Bridge demolition scenes [CUT - treated as absent]
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not contain a bridge demolition sequence, so there is no book baseline being violated. However, the film screenplay contained scenes (235B, 242, 247, 271) in which Seamus is given substantial characterisation — competence, pyrotechnic expertise endorsed by McGonagall, wit, camaraderie with Neville — that constitutes the film's primary attempt to give him individual agency during the battle.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: These scenes were cut from the theatrical release and are excluded from scoring per the non-theatrical material rules. Consequently, the film as released contains no scene in which McGonagall singles out Seamus for a specific task, no scene of him exercising expertise, and no extended comedic-heroic beat with Neville. The only residual trace in the theatrical cut is Trelawney's line 'There's more to me than incense and tea leaves, Mr. Finnegan' (Scenes 11 and 14), which is now contextless.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cut of the bridge sequence eliminates what was, in the screenplay, the film's compensatory mechanism for Seamus's reduced role — his one extended scene of individual heroic function. Its removal leaves a gap: McGonagall's reference to his 'proclivity for pyrotechnics' and Trelawney's line addressing him are orphaned in the theatrical cut, gesturing at characterisation the audience never sees. The book's Patronus scene was already lost; the bridge scene's cut removes the film's own substitute, leaving Seamus with no moment of individual agency in the battle whatsoever.

main_damage_causes: Complete removal of Seamus's only act of individual heroism in the Battle of Hogwarts — the Patronus rescue of Harry, Ron, and Hermione — with no theatrical replacement, eliminating his sole moment of agency and courage in the climax

Invention of a 'Stand down, Neville!' beat that actively recharacterises Seamus as a voice of capitulation at the saga's most critical moment of collective defiance, directly contradicting his book persona as a resolute Gryffindor fighter

Systematic reduction of Seamus's competent, informative, and emotionally textured book dialogue (Room of Requirement briefing, two-weeks-in-hiding account, Dean reunion) to isolated comic relief lines, erasing his standing as a knowledgeable resistance participant and a friend with defined relationships
